# Monitoring Data

## Metadata

Before you download any data, it may be useful to access some key metadata. The following functions are available to do so:

- `import_eea_countries()` accesses country names and codes.

- `import_eea_cities(countries = "FR")` accesses city names in a given country or countries. Note that cities are defined by the EEA using 'Urban Audit' boundaries, which may extend beyond a city's administrative area.

- `import_eea_pollutants()` accesses pollutant names and identifiers.

- `import_eea_stations(countries = "FR")` accesses data flow D (station metadata), such as site names, locations and station types. Note that one or more countries must be specified. This metadata comes from a different source to the rest of the package, which is not a public API, so may occasionally be unavailable.

Each of these functions will return R data frames, making them convenient for further analysis and filtering.

## Downloading Data

To actually download data, you may use `import_eea_monitoring()`. This function has several main arguments:

1. `countries`, requiring a vector of code(s) from `import_eea_countries()`. At least one country must be provided.

2. `cities`, requiring a vector of name(s) from `import_eea_cities()`. If `NULL`, data from all sampling points in the given countries will be imported, including those outside of any city.

3. `pollutants`, requiring a vector of pollutant notation(s) from `import_eea_pollutants()`, such as `"NO2"` or `"PM10"`. If `NULL`, all pollutants will be imported.

4. `datetime_start` and `datetime_end`, which define the period of interest. These can be years (e.g., `2024`), dates (e.g., `as.Date("2024-06-30")`) or exact date-times (e.g., `as.POSIXct("2024-06-30 12:00", tz = "Europe/Paris")`). Years and dates are inclusive, so `datetime_start = 2024` and `datetime_end = 2024` will return the whole of 2024.

5. `dataset`, requiring a value of either `1` (unverified, up-to-date data from data flow E2a), `2` (verified data from data flow E1a), `3` (historical Airbase data), `4` (CAMS forecasts, downscaled to monitoring stations) or `5` (gap-filled E2a data).

6. `aggregation_type`, one of `"hour"`, `"day"` or `"var"` (variable intervals, such as weekly or monthly).

```r
library(euroaq)

aqdata <- import_eea_monitoring(
  countries = "FR",
  cities = "Paris",
  pollutants = c("NO2", "PM10"),
  datetime_start = as.Date("2024-01-01"),
  datetime_end = as.Date("2024-01-31"),
  dataset = 2
)
```

`import_eea_monitoring()` is quite an opinionated function; it renames columns to convenient English names, and binds on commonly useful metadata columns from `import_eea_stations()`. If the station metadata is unavailable, it will warn and return the data without this site information. If a user wants more flexibility, they may wish to access the EEA's API directly (see below).

The EEA limits each download to 600MB. If this limit is reached, `import_eea_monitoring()` will warn that the returned data is incomplete. In this case, either request less data at once, or use `.endpoint = "urls"`, which isn't subject to the limit. This downloads the complete time series of each sampling point, so is slower for short periods, but the data are then filtered to the requested dates and aggregation type, so the result is the same.

## Timezones

The EEA reports hourly and variable data in UTC+01, and daily data in the local time of each station. `import_eea_monitoring()` accounts for this, so the `date` and `date_end` columns always represent the correct instant in time, and the `timezone` column records the timezone each row was reported in. If all rows share a single timezone (e.g., all hourly data) the dates are displayed in that timezone; otherwise they are displayed in UTC.

```r
# convert to another timezone for display, if desired
aqdata$date <- lubridate::with_tz(aqdata$date, "Europe/Paris")
```

## Data Access via API Endpoints

For more flexible data access, including asynchronous data access, there are three options, mirroring the three options outlined in <https://eeadmz1-downloads-webapp.azurewebsites.net/content/documentation/How_To_Downloads.pdf>. Each of these has options to control where data is imported from (countries & cities), specific pollutants to import, and the datasets of origin. Two of the three also allow for users to specify a start and end date, as well as an aggregation type.

- `get_eea_parquet_files()` will download a zip folder of parquet files to a user-specified file, returning the file path.

```r
get_eea_parquet_files(countries = "FR", file = "mydata.zip")

utils::unzip(zipfile = "mydata.zip", exdir = "parquets")

paths <- dir("parquets", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)

tables <- lapply(paths, arrow::read_parquet)

aqdata <- dplyr::bind_rows(tables)
```

- `get_eea_parquet_async()` will initiate the construction of a zip folder of parquet files in the background, and returns a URL at which the zip file will be made available. This is more suitable for larger requests. The file won't exist straight away, so one approach is to check the URL periodically until it does.

```r
zipurl <- get_eea_parquet_async(countries = "FR")

# check every 20 seconds for up to an hour until the file is available
for (i in 1:180) {
  resp <- httr2::request(zipurl) |>
    httr2::req_error(is_error = \(resp) FALSE) |>
    httr2::req_perform(path = "mydata.zip")

  if (httr2::resp_status(resp) != 404) {
    break
  }

  Sys.sleep(20)
}

utils::unzip(zipfile = "mydata.zip", exdir = "parquets")

paths <- dir("parquets", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)

tables <- lapply(paths, arrow::read_parquet)

aqdata <- dplyr::bind_rows(tables)
```

- `get_eea_parquet_urls()` will return an R character vector of URLs at which individual parquet files can be found. Each parquet file contains the complete time series of a single sampling point, so this function ignores the datetime and aggregation type arguments.

```r
urls <- get_eea_parquet_urls(countries = "FR", pollutants = "NO2")

tables <- lapply(urls, arrow::read_parquet)

aqdata <- dplyr::bind_rows(tables)
```

Note that the parquet files contain timezone-less 'clock times'. As described above, hourly data are in UTC+01 and daily data are in the local time of each station.

# Modelled Data

Modelled data at each monitoring station can be accessed using `dataset = 4` in the already discussed functions. Additionally, the EEA Download Portal gives access to complete forecast maps of downscaled CAMS data, for entire countries or capital cities, in raster format. These are available for NO2, O3, PM10 and PM2.5, and only for recent dates. There are two ways to access this:

- Most conveniently, a user can use `import_eea_raster()` which downloads the requested raster files and reads them into R. This requires the `{terra}` package.

- For more flexibility, lower-level API functions are provided - `get_eea_raster_files()` and `get_eea_raster_async()`. These work similarly to their `get_eea_parquet_files()` and `get_eea_parquet_async()` equivalents, already discussed.

The cities available for rasters can be found using `import_eea_cities(modelled = TRUE)`; currently this is each country's capital city. If no city is provided, the raster will cover the entire country.

```r
# which cities are available?
import_eea_cities("FR", modelled = TRUE)

# read yesterday's forecast into R
fr_rast <- import_eea_raster(
  country = "FR",
  city = "Paris",
  pollutants = "PM10",
  datetime_start = Sys.Date() - 1,
  datetime_end = Sys.Date() - 1
)

# each layer is an hour, in UTC
terra::time(fr_rast)

# then can plot or analyse further with {terra}
terra::plet(fr_rast)
```

Note that there is a limit to the width of the date range of data accessed in one time using this approach. The user must also specify a single country and at least one pollutant.
